slides.heading: A hint of the virgin birth?
slides.body: God tells the serpent that a woman’s offspring will crush its head. Some Christians say “her offspring” points to Jesus being born without a human father.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Christians read this as the Bible’s first promise of Jesus. Matthew later says Mary became pregnant through the Holy Spirit, and Jesus is presented as the one who defeats evil.

slides.heading: But Genesis doesn’t say that
slides.body: Genesis never says this child has no human father. It also talks about a woman’s offspring when describing ordinary births. The virgin birth comes from the later Gospel stories—not from this verse.

slides.heading: Is the serpent Satan?
slides.body: Genesis says one of the woman’s descendants will strike the serpent’s head. Christians often read this as Jesus defeating Satan.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Later parts of the Bible call the devil “the ancient serpent” and say Jesus came to destroy his work. So the Christian connection makes sense when the whole Bible is read together.

slides.heading: But that connection comes later
slides.body: Genesis names neither Jesus nor Satan. The story also explains why humans and snakes are enemies. Later writers give the serpent a larger meaning, but Genesis itself does not clearly predict Jesus defeating Satan.

slides.heading: Is Enoch’s disappearance about Jesus?
slides.body: Genesis says Enoch “was no more” because God took him away. Some Christians see this as an early preview of Jesus going up to heaven.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Almost everyone else in this chapter dies. Enoch is the exception, and the New Testament says God took him away without dying. That makes his story look a little like Jesus leaving the earth.

slides.heading: But the stories are different
slides.body: Enoch avoids death. Jesus dies, rises from the dead and then ascends. Genesis does not mention heaven or describe Enoch rising into the sky. The New Testament never says Enoch’s story predicted Jesus.

slides.heading: Did God become Shem’s descendant?
slides.body: Noah calls the LORD “the God of Shem.” Luke later lists Shem among Jesus’s ancestors. Some Christians combine these facts into a prediction that God would join Shem’s family.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Shem’s family line leads to Abraham, Israel and eventually Jesus. The next verse may also picture God living among Shem’s people. For Christians who believe Jesus is God, those details can feel significant.

slides.heading: But that isn’t what Noah says
slides.body: Noah says the LORD is Shem’s God. He never says God will be born as one of Shem’s descendants. Luke supplies Jesus’s family tree, but does not say Noah predicted it.

slides.heading: A promise about Jesus?
slides.body: God promises that every family on earth will be blessed through Abraham. Christians say Jesus is the descendant who brings that blessing to everyone.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Paul calls this promise an early announcement of the good news. He says people from every nation can share Abraham’s blessing through faith in Jesus.

slides.heading: But Genesis says “through you”
slides.body: This verse says the nations will be blessed through Abraham. It does not name Jesus or explain the blessing as faith in him. Paul makes that Christian interpretation later.

slides.heading: Does one “offspring” mean Jesus?
slides.body: God promises land to Abraham’s “offspring.” Paul later points out that the word is singular and says it refers to Christ.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Paul reads all God’s promises to Abraham as reaching their goal in one person: Jesus. People who belong to Jesus then become part of Abraham’s family too.

slides.heading: But the word includes many people
slides.body: Genesis compares this same “offspring” to countless dust and stars. The word is singular but normally describes a whole family. Its grammar alone does not identify Jesus.

slides.heading: A priest like Jesus?
slides.body: Genesis introduces Melchizedek, a man who is both king and priest. Hebrews later says Jesus is a priest forever in the same order.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Melchizedek combines two roles that are usually separate: priest and king. A later Psalm promises another priest like him, and Hebrews says that person is Jesus.

slides.heading: The prediction comes from a Psalm
slides.body: Genesis simply describes a priest who was already alive. The promise of a future priest comes from Psalm 110, not this Genesis verse. Genesis provides the pattern, not the prediction.

slides.heading: Do these titles point to Jesus?
slides.body: The name Melchizedek can be read as “king of righteousness,” and Salem sounds like “peace.” Hebrews connects both ideas with Jesus.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Hebrews compares Melchizedek with the Son of God. A king and priest associated with righteousness and peace makes a striking picture of Jesus.

slides.heading: But they describe Melchizedek
slides.body: In Genesis, the name and title belong to Melchizedek himself. Nothing there says a future person will carry the same meaning. Hebrews makes the connection later.

slides.heading: A preview of the Last Supper?
slides.body: Melchizedek brings out bread and wine. Jesus later shares bread and wine at the Last Supper. Christians have connected the two meals for centuries.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Hebrews already compares Melchizedek’s priesthood with Jesus. That made his bread and wine a natural symbol of Communion for early Christians.

slides.heading: But Genesis describes a meal
slides.body: Genesis does not call the bread and wine a sacrifice or say they predict a future meal. Hebrews discusses Melchizedek at length but never mentions them. The link arose later.

slides.heading: Does Isaac’s family point to Jesus?
slides.body: God promises that his agreement with Abraham will continue through Isaac’s descendants. Luke later places Jesus in that family line.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: God chooses Isaac’s family for this special promise. Paul calls them the children of promise, and Luke confirms that Jesus belongs to the same family.

slides.heading: But Jesus isn’t the only descendant
slides.body: Genesis predicts Isaac and a large family after him. It does not identify one future Messiah. Jesus fits the family line, but so do many other people.

slides.heading: Did God promise Jesus as the lamb?
slides.body: Abraham tells Isaac that God will provide a lamb. A ram is then killed instead of Isaac. John later calls Jesus “the Lamb of God.”

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: A beloved son faces death, but God provides another victim in his place. Christians see this as a powerful preview of God giving Jesus to save others.

slides.heading: But the story gives its own answer
slides.body: God provides a ram for that day’s sacrifice. John never says he is referring to Isaac’s story, and his lamb image could come from several other Bible passages.

slides.heading: One descendant who blesses everyone?
slides.body: Genesis says every nation will be blessed through Abraham’s offspring. Acts applies that promise to Jesus.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: This verse joins Abraham’s descendants with worldwide blessing. Acts and Paul both present Jesus as the descendant through whom that blessing reaches other nations.

slides.heading: But “offspring” means a family too
slides.body: The previous verse compares Abraham’s offspring to countless stars and grains of sand. Genesis does not identify one person. Acts and Paul focus the promise on Jesus later.

slides.heading: Was a rescuer promised through Isaac?
slides.body: God repeats Abraham’s promises to Isaac. Some Christian lists say this predicts that Jesus, the rescuer, would come from Isaac’s family.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: The promises of land, a huge family and worldwide blessing pass through Isaac. Christians believe Jesus is the person who eventually brings that blessing to everyone.

slides.heading: But these verses promise a family
slides.body: Genesis speaks of many descendants, not one named rescuer. The passage in Hebrews is about Isaac’s family continuing. It does not say these verses predicted Jesus.

slides.heading: Is Jesus Jacob’s ladder?
slides.body: Jacob dreams of angels moving between earth and heaven. Jesus later says angels will rise and descend on the Son of Man.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: The repeated image is hard to miss. Jesus places himself at the centre of the scene, so Christians see him as the meeting point between heaven and earth.

slides.heading: But Genesis is about Jacob
slides.body: Jacob’s dream assures him that God is with him and will keep promises about his family and land. It does not predict a future person. Jesus gives the image a new meaning later.

slides.heading: Does Jacob’s “offspring” mean Jesus?
slides.body: God promises Jacob a huge family that will bless the world. Luke later includes Jacob in Jesus’s family tree.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Jesus belongs to the family through which God promised blessing. Christians therefore see him as the descendant who represents Israel and brings that blessing to other nations.

slides.heading: But a family tree proves very little
slides.body: Genesis explicitly promises many descendants. Luke confirms that Jesus is one of them, but does not connect this verse with him. Countless other descendants meet the same test.

slides.heading: Did Genesis predict when Jesus would come?
slides.body: Genesis says Judah will keep the royal sceptre “until Shiloh comes.” Some Christians treat this as a deadline for God’s promised ruler to arrive.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: The verse can be read as promising a future ruler from Judah. Jesus is from Judah’s royal family, and Christians believe he arrived at God’s chosen time.

slides.heading: But there is no clear deadline
slides.body: Experts disagree about what “Shiloh” means, and the verse never defines when Judah loses the sceptre. The New Testament passages do not supply the missing date.

slides.heading: Was Jesus promised through Judah?
slides.body: Jacob says the royal sceptre belongs to Judah. Luke later lists Judah among Jesus’s ancestors.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: The blessing points toward a ruler from Judah, and some early Jewish readers understood it as a promise about a future king. Jesus comes from the right family.

slides.heading: But the family is enormous
slides.body: Judah has many descendants. Genesis does not predict one particular birth, and Luke never says Jesus fulfils this verse. The ancestry fits, but it cannot identify him by itself.

slides.heading: Was Jesus’s name predicted?
slides.body: Some translations say a ruler called “Shiloh” will come. The claim says Shiloh means “the one sent,” a title that points to Jesus.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: The verse can be read as promising a future ruler. Jesus repeatedly says God sent him, so “the one sent” sounds like a good match.

slides.heading: But “sent” is not a secure meaning
slides.body: The Hebrew word is difficult, and many translations do not treat Shiloh as a name at all. John never calls Jesus Shiloh or says this verse predicted him.

slides.heading: A deadline before Judah disappeared?
slides.body: The claim says God’s promised ruler had to arrive before Judah lost its identity. Genesis actually talks about Judah keeping a sceptre and ruler’s staff.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: If the verse promises a ruler from Judah, Jesus arrives while Jewish leaders and institutions still exist. That can look like the promise reaching its goal in time.

slides.heading: But rule is not identity
slides.body: Losing political power is not the same as a tribe ceasing to exist. Genesis gives no deadline based on tribal identity, and the passage in John does not add one.

slides.heading: One ruler for many nations?
slides.body: Genesis pictures nations obeying a ruler from Judah. Jesus speaks of other sheep joining one flock under one shepherd.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Both passages picture people gathering under one leader. Christians see Jesus bringing people from outside Israel into the community he leads.

slides.heading: But the pictures are not identical
slides.body: John never quotes Genesis here. A flock listening to one shepherd is not the same as nations obeying a king. The ideas are similar, but the match does not identify Jesus by itself.

slides.heading: Did Jesus use God’s name?
slides.body: God tells Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” Jesus later says, “Before Abraham was born, I am.” Christians hear an echo of God’s name.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Jesus contrasts his existence with Abraham’s, and his listeners try to stone him. That makes the statement sound like a bold claim to share God’s identity.

slides.heading: But Exodus is not predicting Jesus
slides.body: Exodus reveals God’s name during Moses’s story. It says nothing about a future saviour. Jesus may echo this or other passages, but that is a later claim about his identity—not an Exodus prediction.

slides.heading: A spotless lamb like Jesus?
slides.body: The Passover animal had to be free from defects. The New Testament describes Jesus as an unblemished offering.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Christians see the flawless Passover animal as a picture of Jesus’s sinless life and sacrifice. The New Testament itself uses both lamb and sacrifice language for him.

slides.heading: But this was a ritual rule
slides.body: Exodus tells families how to choose an animal for Passover. It could be a sheep or a goat, and other sacrifices also had to be free from defects. The rule does not uniquely predict Jesus.

slides.heading: Does Passover blood point to Jesus?
slides.body: Israelite families marked their doors with blood and escaped a deadly plague. Paul says Jesus’s blood saves people from God’s judgement.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Both stories involve blood and rescue from death or judgement. Christians see Passover as an early picture of salvation through Jesus’s sacrifice.

slides.heading: But the rescues are different
slides.body: In Exodus, the blood protects households during a plague. The passage says nothing about forgiveness of sins. Paul does not mention Passover in the verses used for this claim.

slides.heading: Paul calls Jesus our Passover lamb
slides.body: Exodus describes the Passover sacrifice that spared Israelite homes. Paul later writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”

slides.heading: This connection is explicit
slides.body: Paul continues the Passover picture by telling Christians to remove the “leaven” of bad behaviour. He clearly wants his readers to connect Jesus with the festival.

slides.heading: But Exodus had its own meaning
slides.body: Passover remembers God rescuing families from Egypt. Paul later gives that story a Christian meaning. His comparison is clear, but Exodus itself was not predicting Jesus.

slides.heading: Jesus’s bones were not broken
slides.body: Exodus says the Passover animal’s bones must not be broken. John says soldiers left Jesus’s legs unbroken and calls it a fulfilment of Scripture.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: The match is unusually exact, and John makes it himself. He presents Jesus as a new Passover sacrifice whose bones remain unbroken.

slides.heading: But Exodus gives a meal rule
slides.body: Exodus tells people how to prepare the Passover animal, not how a future Messiah will die. A similar rule appears in Numbers, and a Psalm also mentions unbroken bones.

slides.heading: Is Jesus’s name hidden here?
slides.body: Exodus says the LORD became Israel’s “salvation.” Jesus’s Hebrew name comes from the same family of words.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Matthew explains Jesus’s name by saying he will save his people. Christians can see God’s rescue from Egypt as an early picture of the salvation they find in Jesus.

slides.heading: But “salvation” is not a name
slides.body: The Hebrew word in Exodus is an ordinary word meaning salvation, not the name Yeshua. The song celebrates a rescue that has already happened.

slides.heading: Does God’s holiness predict Jesus?
slides.body: Exodus praises the LORD as “majestic in holiness.” Luke calls Jesus the Holy One, and Acts calls him God’s holy servant.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Christians believe Jesus shows people what God is like. A holy saviour who shares God’s character makes sense within that belief.

slides.heading: But the song is about God
slides.body: Exodus praises the LORD for rescuing Israel from Egypt. It does not describe a future saviour. Jesus may share that holiness, but the song does not predict him.

slides.heading: Paul says the rock was Christ
slides.body: God gives Israel water from a rock in the desert. Paul later says the spiritual rock that travelled with them “was Christ.”

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: God stands by the rock, and the story asks whether the LORD is with Israel. Christians read Paul as saying Christ was God’s presence with them.

slides.heading: But Exodus is not a forecast
slides.body: Exodus describes water supplied during an emergency. It never names a future saviour or says the stone travelled with Israel. Paul gives the story a Christian meaning later.

slides.heading: Does this predict Jesus’s mercy?
slides.body: God tells Moses that he will show mercy and compassion. Luke later celebrates God’s mercy as the promised rescuer arrives.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Luke says God raises a saviour from David’s family. Christians believe Jesus is how God’s promised mercy reaches the world.

slides.heading: But both verses describe God
slides.body: God speaks about his own mercy in Exodus, and God is the one showing mercy in Luke. Jesus may bring that mercy, but Exodus is not predicting his personality.

slides.heading: A sacrifice pleasing to God?
slides.body: Leviticus calls a burnt offering “a pleasing aroma to the LORD.” Ephesians describes Jesus giving himself to God as a fragrant sacrifice.

slides.heading: Why Christians connect them
slides.body: Ephesians deliberately uses language familiar from Israel’s sacrifices. Christians see Jesus’s self-giving as the perfect offering those older rituals pointed towards.

slides.heading: But this phrase was used often
slides.body: Leviticus uses “pleasing aroma” for many repeated offerings. It does not single out one future sacrifice. Ephesians later applies the familiar image to Jesus.
